title: DevOps from Scratch: Git, CI, Containers, Kubernetes and Reliability
subtitle: From commit to production, with a working simulator of git, docker, kubectl and a pipeline in every lab
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A condensed, original course on DevOps. It covers the culture and the DORA metrics, Git and branching, continuous integration, build artifacts and semantic versioning, containers and Dockerfiles, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, configuration and secrets, release strategies, monitoring, SLOs and incidents, DevSecOps, and a capstone that takes a change from bug to production. Every shell lab runs a Linux-like simulator inside the app, with simplified git, docker, kubectl, make, a CI runner and an infrastructure tool. These are teaching simulators, not the real programs, so they behave like the real tools in the common cases only. Credits: BusyBox (GPL-2.0) and the Jade Agent Kit (MIT).

chapters.title: What DevOps is
summary: DevOps is a way of working in which the people who build software and the people who run it share responsibility and tools. The goal is to deliver changes to users quickly, safely and repeatedly.
It rests on a few habits: keep everything in version control, automate builds, tests and deployment, ship small changes often, and watch what happens in production so you can learn fast.
Four measures from the DORA research show how a team is doing: how often it deploys, how long a change takes to reach users, how often changes fail, and how fast it recovers.

glossary.def: An automated path that takes a change from commit to production.
Repetitive manual work that grows with the service and could be automated.
The time from a commit to that change running in production.
The share of deployments that cause a problem needing a fix or rollback.

keyPoints: Share responsibility between building and running.
Automate everything you do more than twice.
Small, frequent changes are safer than big rare ones.
Measure: frequency, lead time, failure rate, recovery time.

items: ELI5. DevOps is like a kitchen where the cooks and the waiters work as one team. They hand out small plates often, and they listen to how the guests liked them.
Before DevOps, developers often wrote code and threw it over a wall to an operations team, who had to run something they had never seen. Releases were big, rare and scary. DevOps tears down the wall.
A team owns a service from the first line of code to the pager at night, and uses automation to make releases boring.

Four ideas carry most of the weight. First, put everything in version control: code, configuration, infrastructure and pipeline definitions. Second, automate the path to production so that a change is built, tested and deployed the same way every time.
Third, ship small changes often, because a small change is easy to understand and easy to undo. Fourth, observe the running system and feed what you learn back into the next change.

The DORA research programme found that four numbers separate high-performing teams from the rest. Deployment frequency is how often you release. Lead time for changes is how long a commit takes to reach production. Change failure rate is the share of releases that cause trouble.
Time to restore service is how long it takes to recover. Notably, the best teams are better at all four at once: speed and stability do not trade off.

DevOps is not a job title or a single tool. Tools such as Git, Docker, Kubernetes and Terraform help, but the heart of it is culture: blameless reviews, shared ownership and a habit of automating pain away. The rest of this course takes the tools one at a time, in the order a change travels.

chapters.title: Git: tracking every change
summary: Git is a distributed version control system. It records every change as a commit, a snapshot of your files with a message, and links the commits into a history.
The everyday cycle is: edit files, git add to stage them, git commit to record them. git status tells you where things stand and git log shows the history.
A commit has an id, an author, a message and a pointer to its parent. That chain of parents is the history, and it is what makes undo, review and collaboration possible.

glossary.def: A saved snapshot of the tracked files, with a message and a parent.
Also called the index: the changes you have selected for the next commit.
The actual files in your folder.
Another copy of the repository, for example on a server.

keyPoints: Write commit messages that say why.

items: ELI5. Git is a time machine for your files. Every save is a numbered photo with a note, so you can look back at any day or undo a mistake.
Git keeps three areas. The working tree holds the files you edit. The staging area holds the changes you have chosen for the next commit. The repository holds the committed history.
git add copies changes from the working tree to the staging area, and git commit turns the staging area into a new commit.

lesson.code:
git init                       # start a repository here
git status                     # what changed?
git add app.py                 # stage one file (or . for all)
git commit -m "Add greeting"   # record it
git log --oneline              # the history, newest first
git diff                       # unstaged changes
git diff --staged              # staged changes

items: The staging area lets you build a commit from just the changes that belong together, even if you edited many files. Write the message as a short summary of the change and, if needed, why you made it. A good history reads like a changelog.

Every commit has a unique id, a long hash of its contents and its parent. Because the id depends on the history before it, nobody can change an old commit without changing all the ids after it. That makes the history trustworthy and lets two people compare their copies by comparing ids.

chapters.title: Branches, merges and conflicts
summary: A branch is a lightweight pointer to a commit. You create one to work on a feature without disturbing the main line, then merge it back when it is ready.
If main has not moved since you branched, merging just slides the pointer forward, which is a fast-forward. If both sides changed, git makes a merge commit with two parents.
When both sides changed the same lines, git cannot decide and marks a conflict. You edit the file, choose the right result, add it and commit.

glossary.def: A named pointer to a commit that moves forward as you commit.
Combining the work of two branches into one.
Overlapping changes that git cannot combine automatically.
A request to merge a branch, with discussion and review.

keyPoints: Branch for every piece of work.
A conflict is normal, not an error.

items: ELI5. A branch is a side road. You try your idea there so the main road stays clear, and then you merge back. If two roads changed the same sign, you pick the right one.

lesson.code:
git branch                  # list branches
git checkout -b feature     # create and switch
# ...edit, add, commit...
git checkout main           # switch back
git merge feature           # bring the work in
git log --oneline           # see the merge

items: Branches are cheap, so use them freely. A feature branch keeps unfinished work away from the code everyone else uses. In a team flow, you open a pull request, colleagues review it, an automated pipeline checks it and then it is merged.
The best branches live for hours or days, not weeks, because the longer they live the more they drift from main.

A conflict happens when two branches changed the same part of the same file. Git stops and writes both versions into the file between markers: the lines after the first marker are yours, the lines after the equals line are theirs, and the closing marker ends the block.
You edit the file to the result you want, delete the markers, run git add on the file and then git commit.

lesson.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
title: Main
=======
title: Feature
>>>>>>> feature

chapters.title: Continuous integration
summary: Continuous integration means merging small changes into the shared branch often, and letting an automated pipeline build and test every one of them.
A pipeline is a list of stages that run in order, such as build, test and package. If any stage fails, the pipeline stops and tells you which one, so a broken change never reaches the main line.
Good pipelines are fast, reliable and the single source of truth about whether the code works.

glossary.def: The automated sequence of stages run for each change.
One step of a pipeline, such as build or test.
The machine that executes a pipeline's jobs.
A test that sometimes fails for no real reason and erodes trust.

keyPoints: Run the pipeline on every commit.
A red pipeline blocks the merge.
Fix flaky tests, do not ignore them.

items: ELI5. A robot checks your homework every time you hand it in. It builds your model and tests it, and if something is wrong it stops and tells you which step failed.

Continuous integration is a habit and a machine. The habit is to merge to the main branch at least daily. The machine is a server that, on every push, checks out the code, builds it, runs the tests and reports the result.
Problems are found minutes after they are introduced, when the change is still fresh in mind.

lesson.code:
# pipeline.txt: one stage per line, 'name: command'
lint:   test -s app.py
build:  echo compiling
test:   grep -q "a + b" app.py
deploy: echo shipping to staging

# stages run in order, the first failure stops the rest

items: Order stages so that the cheapest and fastest checks come first. A linter that takes a second should run before a test suite that takes ten minutes. Use caching so unchanged work is not repeated.
Run independent jobs in parallel, but keep the pipeline definition itself in version control next to the code.

A pipeline you cannot trust is worse than none. A flaky test that fails one run in twenty teaches people to press retry and ignore red. Fix it or delete it. Treat a failing main branch as an emergency, because everyone's work is now blocked.

chapters.title: Build, test and release artifacts

maps.title: Artifacts
links: Reproducible | means | Same inputs, same output

summary: A build turns source code into an artifact: a package, a binary or a container image. The same artifact should travel unchanged through every environment, so what you tested is what you ship.
Version numbers follow semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Increase PATCH for fixes, MINOR for compatible features and MAJOR for breaking changes.
Tests come in layers: many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and a handful of end-to-end checks. The pipeline runs them from fastest to slowest.

glossary.def: A built output stored for deployment, such as a package or image.
A MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH scheme where each part signals the kind of change.
A server that stores and serves artifacts.
A build that gives the same result from the same inputs.

keyPoints: PATCH fixes, MINOR features, MAJOR breaks.
Many unit tests, few end-to-end tests.

items: ELI5. Bake the cake once, put a label on it with a number, and serve that same cake everywhere. Add one to the number for a fix, a bigger step for a new flavour.

The rule is build once, deploy many. You build an artifact a single time in the pipeline, give it a unique version, store it in a registry and then promote that same artifact through test, staging and production. If you rebuild for each environment you are no longer deploying what you tested.

lesson.code:
# a tiny Makefile; run it with: make test
build:
	echo compiling
test: build
	echo running tests

grep -q 'a + b' app.py    # a one-line test: exit 0 means pass

items: Semantic versioning gives numbers a meaning. Version 2.4.1 means major 2, minor 4, patch 1. A fix that changes no behaviour bumps the patch to 2.4.2. A new feature that keeps old users working bumps the minor and resets the patch to 2.5.0.
A change that breaks existing users bumps the major and resets both: 3.0.0.

Tests are a pyramid. At the bottom are unit tests: fast, many, each checking one small thing. Above them are integration tests that check parts working together. At the top are a few end-to-end tests that drive the whole system.
The higher you go, the slower and more fragile the tests, so keep the top thin.

chapters.title: Containers and Docker
summary: A container packages an application with everything it needs to run, and runs it isolated from other processes using features of the Linux kernel. It starts in a fraction of a second and behaves the same on any machine.
An image is the read-only template, a container is a running instance of it. You pull images from a registry, run them, stop them and remove them.
Ports are mapped from the host to the container, so a web server inside can be reached from outside.

glossary.def: A read-only template containing a filesystem and settings.
A running (or stopped) instance of an image.
The most common tool for building and running containers.
Connecting a host port to a port inside a container, such as -p 8080:80.

keyPoints: Image is the recipe, container is the dish.
docker run image starts a container.
Containers are disposable: keep data outside.

items: ELI5. A container is a lunch box with the food, the fork and the napkin all packed. It works the same at any table. The image is the recipe card for the lunch box.
A virtual machine carries a whole operating system. A container shares the host's kernel and only brings the files and libraries your program needs, so it is small and starts almost instantly.
The kernel keeps containers apart using namespaces, which give each its own view of processes, network and filesystem, and control groups, which limit CPU and memory.

lesson.code:
docker pull nginx                       # fetch an image
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx   # start it in the background
docker ps                                # running containers
curl http://localhost:8080               # talk to it
docker logs web                          # its output
docker stop web                          # stop it
docker rm web                            # remove it

items: The flag -d runs the container in the background, --name gives it a name you can use later, and -p 8080:80 sends traffic arriving at port 8080 on your machine to port 80 inside. Without -p the container's ports are not reachable from outside.
docker ps shows running containers, and docker ps -a also shows stopped ones.

Treat containers as disposable. When you need a change, you build a new image and replace the container rather than logging in and patching it. Anything that must survive, such as a database's files, goes in a volume outside the container. This is what makes containers easy to scale and replace.

chapters.title: Dockerfiles and image layers
summary: A Dockerfile is a recipe for an image. Each instruction adds a layer: FROM chooses the base, COPY adds files, RUN executes a command during the build, and CMD says what runs when the container starts.
Docker caches layers. If an instruction and everything before it are unchanged, the cached layer is reused. Once one step changes, every step after it is rebuilt.
So order matters: put things that change rarely, such as installing dependencies, before things that change often, such as your own code.

glossary.def: A text file of instructions that builds an image.
The filesystem change made by one instruction; layers stack.
Stored layers reused when a step and its predecessors are unchanged.
The starting image named in FROM.

keyPoints: Order from least to most frequently changing.
Do not run as root in the container.

items: ELI5. A Dockerfile is a recipe in layers like a sandwich. If you change the top slice, you keep all the bottom layers and only redo the top one.

lesson.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY requirements.txt /app/
RUN pip install -r /app/requirements.txt
COPY app.py /app/
CMD python app.py

items: Read this Dockerfile top to bottom. FROM starts from a small Python image. The requirements file is copied first and the dependencies are installed. Only then is the application code copied.

When you edit app.py, the first three layers are unchanged and come from the cache, so only the last COPY and CMD run again. If you had copied all the code before installing, every code edit would reinstall every dependency.
The cache key for a step includes the instruction text, the layers before it and, for COPY, the contents of the files. That is why changing one early line forces everything after it to rebuild.
Small images start faster and have fewer things that can be attacked, so use slim base images, avoid leaving build tools behind and add a .dockerignore file.

lesson.code:
docker build -t myapp:1 .     # build and tag
docker images                  # list local images
docker run -d --name app myapp:1
docker logs app

chapters.title: Kubernetes

maps.title: Kubernetes
links: Replica | is | A copy of a pod

summary: Kubernetes runs containers across many machines. You do not start containers by hand. You describe the state you want, for example three copies of this image, and Kubernetes works constantly to make reality match.
A pod is the smallest unit and holds one or more containers. A deployment keeps a set number of identical pods running and rolls out new versions. A service gives them one stable address.
Because Kubernetes compares desired and actual state in a loop, it heals itself: if a pod dies, a new one appears.

glossary.def: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing a network.
A controller that keeps a desired number of identical pods running.
A stable address and load balancer in front of pods.
A YAML file that declares a desired object.

keyPoints: Declare the desired state; Kubernetes converges.
Deployments own pods; services find pods.

items: ELI5. Kubernetes is a manager who always checks that three workers are on shift. If one goes home sick, the manager calls in a new one straight away.

The core idea of Kubernetes is the control loop. You write down what you want in a manifest and apply it. Controllers then watch the real state and act to remove any difference. Delete a pod and the deployment notices it is short by one and creates another.
This is called declarative configuration, in contrast to imperative commands that say do this step now.

lesson.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: nginx:1.25
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  ports:
  - port: 80
  selector:
    app: web

kubectl apply -f dep.yaml                 # create or update from the file
kubectl get pods                           # what is running
kubectl scale deployment web --replicas=4  # more copies
kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:1.27   # roll out a new version
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web        # go back if it is broken
kubectl delete pod NAME                    # it comes back

items: A rolling update replaces pods a few at a time, so the service stays up. If the new version is broken, for example the image cannot be pulled, the new pods never become ready and the old ones keep serving. rollout undo returns to the previous version.
get pods shows STATUS values such as Running and ImagePullBackOff, and describe pod shows the events that explain them.

chapters.title: Infrastructure as code
summary: Infrastructure as code means servers, networks and databases are described in files and created by tools, not by clicking in a console. The files live in version control and are reviewed like any other code.
A good tool works in two steps. Plan compares the files with what exists and shows the difference. Apply makes the world match the files. Running apply twice changes nothing the second time.
That property, idempotence, is what makes automation safe to run again and again.

glossary.def: Describing the end state you want rather than the steps to reach it.
The tool's record of the resources it created.
When real infrastructure differs from the code, usually after a manual change.
Replacing servers with new ones instead of modifying them.

items: ELI5. Instead of building your toy city by hand each time, you write a plan. The plan can build the whole city again, and building twice changes nothing new.

Clicking through a console is quick once and impossible to repeat exactly. Code can be reviewed, tested, copied to make a second environment and rolled back through version control. Tools such as Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi and CloudFormation turn a description of resources into API calls.

lesson.code:
# infra.txt: one resource per line, 'type name properties'
server web size=small
db main size=large

iac plan     # + server.web, + db.main
iac apply    # creates them
iac apply    # No changes. Infrastructure matches the configuration.

items: The plan lists what would be created with a plus, changed with a tilde and destroyed with a minus. Read it before every apply: a surprising minus is the thing the review exists to catch.
The state file lets the tool know which real resources belong to which lines of code, so protect it and keep it in a shared, locked place.

Drift happens when someone changes a resource by hand. The next plan shows the difference and apply corrects it. Many teams go further and forbid manual changes entirely. Servers become cattle, not pets: if one is wrong you replace it from code instead of nursing it.

chapters.title: Configuration and secrets
summary: The same build runs in development, staging and production, so what differs between them must be configuration kept outside the code: addresses, feature flags and credentials.
Environment variables are the simplest way to pass configuration into a program. Settings are layered: defaults in code, then a config file, then environment variables, with later layers winning.
Secrets such as passwords and API keys need extra care: never commit them, store them in a secrets manager, give them the least access needed and rotate them.

glossary.def: A named value passed to a process by its environment.
A credential such as a password, token or private key.
A service that stores secrets, controls access and logs use.
Regularly replacing a secret so a leaked one stops working.

keyPoints: Code is the same everywhere; config differs.

items: ELI5. Settings go on sticky notes outside the machine, and secrets go in a locked box. You never write a password on the wall of the shop.

The twelve-factor approach to building applications says to store configuration in the environment. The code reads DATABASE_URL and does not care whether it points at a test database or the real one. The same artifact, with different variables, becomes a different environment.

lesson.code:
# layered settings: later wins
defaults:  port=8080 debug=false
file:      port=9090
env:       DEBUG=true
=> port=9090 debug=true

export API_URL=https://staging.example.com
./app

items: A secret committed to Git is compromised forever. Even after you delete it, it stays in the history, and bots scan public repositories for keys within minutes. Keep secrets out of the repository and out of images.
Put them in a secrets manager or in your platform's secret store, and inject them at run time.

If a secret does leak, the fix is not to delete the commit but to revoke the secret and issue a new one. Make this easy by rotating secrets on a schedule, scoping each one to the least access it needs and keeping an audit log of who used it.

chapters.title: Continuous delivery and release strategies
summary: Continuous delivery means every change that passes the pipeline could be released at any moment. Continuous deployment goes one step further and releases automatically.

Release safely by exposing a change gradually. A canary sends a small share of traffic to the new version and watches the errors. Blue-green keeps two full environments and switches between them. Feature flags separate deploying code from turning a feature on.
Whatever the method, you need a fast, rehearsed way back: a rollback must be one command, not a project.

glossary.def: Sending a small percentage of traffic to a new version before everyone.
Running old and new environments side by side and switching traffic.
A switch that turns a feature on or off without deploying.
Returning to the previous known good version.

keyPoints: Deploy is not release: flags separate them.
Start with a few percent, then widen.
Watch error rate and latency during rollout.

items: ELI5. When you release a new game level, first let a few friends try it. If they like it, let everyone in. If not, close the door and go back to the old level.
Deploying means putting code on servers. Releasing means exposing it to users. Treating them as separate steps is what makes releases calm.
With a feature flag the new code ships switched off, you turn it on for staff, then for one percent of users, then everyone, and if something is wrong you flip the switch back without a deployment.

A canary release starts the new version on a few instances, say five percent of traffic, and compares its error rate and speed with the old version. If it looks as good, the share grows in steps until everyone has it. If it looks worse, the canary is removed and most users never noticed.
Blue-green keeps two production environments. You deploy to the idle one, test it, then switch the router. Rollback is switching back.

lesson.code:
kubectl set image deployment/web web=nginx:1.27   # rolling update
kubectl rollout status deployment/web
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web                # roll back

items: Rollouts need data to be safe. A pipeline should check health after each step and stop on its own when the error rate rises. Database changes are the hard part: make them backward compatible, in small steps, so both versions can run at once.

practice.title: Canary decision
practice.intro: Write canary(new_requests, new_errors, base_requests, base_errors, margin). If the canary has seen fewer than 100 requests return 'wait'. Otherwise compare error rates (errors divided by requests): return 'promote' if the canary rate is at most the baseline rate plus margin, else 'rollback'.
practice.hint: Compute both error rates as fractions and compare with the margin.

chapters.title: Monitoring and observability
summary: You cannot run what you cannot see. Observability rests on three kinds of data: metrics, which are numbers over time; logs, which are records of events; and traces, which follow a single request through many services.
For averages, use percentiles. The 99th percentile latency says how slow the slowest one in a hundred requests is, and that is what unhappy users feel.
Alert on symptoms that users notice, such as errors and slowness, not on every internal number, or people will learn to ignore the pager.

glossary.def: A numeric measurement sampled over time, such as requests per second.
A timestamped record of something that happened.
The path and timing of one request across services.
The value below which a given share of measurements fall.

keyPoints: Metrics, logs and traces answer different questions.
Average hides pain; look at p95 and p99.

items: ELI5. Dashboards are the lights on a car. Logs are the diary, and traces follow one marble through a maze. Look at the slowest marbles, not only the average.

Metrics are cheap and tell you that something is wrong: error rate is up. Logs tell you what happened in detail: this request failed with a timeout. Traces tell you where the time went across services: the delay is in the payment call.
You use them in that order, from the dashboard to the log to the trace.

Averages lie. If ninety-nine requests take 100 milliseconds and one takes ten seconds, the average is about 200 milliseconds and looks fine, but one user in a hundred waited ten seconds. Percentiles describe the tail.
The 50th percentile is the median, the 95th is the value that 95 percent of requests beat, and the 99th shows the worst experiences.

lesson.code:
# each log line: time status latency_ms
awk '{print $3}' app.log | sort -n | tail -1      # slowest
grep -c ' 5[0-9][0-9] ' app.log                    # server errors
awk '$2 >= 500 {e++} END {print e / NR * 100}' app.log   # error percent

items: An alert should mean a human must act now. Page on symptoms, such as the error rate is above the target or the site is slow, rather than causes, such as CPU is at 80 percent, which may be harmless. Every alert needs a runbook, a short document that says what it means and what to do.
If an alert fires often and nobody acts, delete it or fix its cause.

practice.title: Percentile
practice.intro: Write percentile(values, p) using the nearest-rank method: sort the values, compute rank = ceil(p / 100 * n) with a minimum of 1, and return the value at that rank (counting from 1). Return 0 for an empty list.
practice.hint: Nearest rank: round the position up, then subtract one for zero-based indexing.

chapters.title: SLOs, error budgets and incidents
summary: A service level indicator, SLI, is a measurement of how well a service works, for instance the share of requests that succeed. A service level objective, SLO, is the target for it, such as 99.9 percent over 30 days.
The gap between perfect and the SLO is the error budget. While budget remains you can ship quickly; when it runs out you slow down and fix reliability.
When something breaks, handle it as an incident: one person leads, you communicate, you restore service first and investigate afterwards, then write a blameless postmortem.

glossary.def: Service level indicator: a measured value such as the success rate.
Service level objective: the target for an SLI.
The amount of failure the SLO allows in a period.
A written, blameless review of an incident and what to change.

keyPoints: Spend budget on change; protect it when low.
Restore first, find the cause second.

items: ELI5. A promise of 99.9 percent leaves a small allowance for mistakes, like a few free passes. Use them to try new things, and stop when they run out.

Perfect reliability is impossible and absurdly expensive, and users cannot tell the difference between 99.99 percent and 100 percent. So you pick a target that is good enough, for example 99.9 percent of requests succeed over thirty days.
That is the SLO, and everything you do is balanced against it.

With a 99.9 percent SLO and one million requests in the period, the budget is one thousand failed requests. If you have used four hundred, you have six hundred left. A fast burn tells you to stop risky releases and fix the cause.
A budget barely touched means you may be too cautious and can release faster. This turns the argument between speed and stability into arithmetic.

During an incident, name an incident lead, open a channel, tell users what you know, and focus on restoring service, often by rolling back, before hunting the root cause. Afterwards, write a postmortem.

A good one describes the timeline, the impact and the contributing causes, and ends with concrete actions. It asks what in the system allowed this to happen, not who made the mistake. Blame teaches people to hide problems, and hidden problems come back bigger.

practice.title: Error budget
practice.intro: Write error_budget(slo, total, failed) where slo is a percentage such as 99.9, total the number of requests and failed the number that failed. Return [allowed failures rounded down to a whole number, remaining budget as a whole number which may be negative]. Allowed is (100 - slo) / 100 * total.
practice.hint: Allowed failures are the non-SLO share of the total; remaining is allowed minus failed.

chapters.title: DevSecOps and the software supply chain
summary: DevSecOps builds security into the pipeline instead of adding it at the end. Scanning for secrets, vulnerable dependencies and risky configuration runs on every change, where fixes are cheap.
Modern software is mostly other people's code. A software bill of materials lists every component so that when a flaw is announced you can find out at once whether you use it.
Protect the pipeline itself: sign artifacts, use short-lived credentials, run containers as non-root users and give each job the least access it needs.

glossary.def: Doing security checks earlier in the process, nearer to the commit.
Software bill of materials: a list of the components in a build.
A public identifier for a known vulnerability.
Compromising software by attacking something it depends on or the way it is built.

keyPoints: Scan every commit for secrets and known vulnerable dependencies.

items: ELI5. Lock the doors early: look for secrets in your code, check the parts you borrowed for known problems, and never wear the master key at the shop counter.
Finding a security problem in a pull request costs minutes. Finding it in production costs an incident.

So checks run early: a secret scanner looks for keys in each commit, a dependency scanner compares your libraries to a database of known vulnerabilities, and a linter for container and infrastructure files flags risky settings such as running as root.

lesson.code:
grep -rn 'API_KEY\|PASSWORD\|secret' .     # crude secret hunt
sed -i 's/sk_live_abc123/${API_KEY}/' app.conf    # move it to an env var
echo '.env' >> .gitignore                          # never commit it

# Dockerfile: do not run as root
RUN adduser --system app
USER app

items: Most of your code is dependencies, and each one is a way in. Pin versions so builds are repeatable, update them regularly and let a scanner tell you when one is vulnerable.
Keep a software bill of materials so that when the next big flaw is announced you can answer in minutes whether you are affected.

Attackers also target the build. Use short-lived credentials rather than long-lived keys, give each pipeline job only the access it needs, require review for changes to pipeline files, and sign artifacts so that production can check that an image really came from your pipeline.

chapters.title: Capstone: ship a change end to end
summary: Put the whole path together. A small project has a bug, a pipeline, a Dockerfile and a Kubernetes manifest. You will fix the bug, make the pipeline pass, build a versioned image and roll it out.
Work like a DevOps engineer: change one thing at a time, check the result of each step, and keep everything in version control.
When the checklist is complete you will have touched version control, CI, containers and orchestration on one change.

glossary.def: A specific version of the software made available to users.
The process of replacing the running version with a new one.
A record of how and from what an artifact was built.
Manual repeated work that a pipeline should do instead.

keyPoints: Tag images with a version, not latest.

items: ELI5. Be the pit crew: fix the bug, test it, pack it in a labelled box, send it out, and watch the dials. If the car shakes, swap back to the old tyres.

A real change flows through every chapter of this course. You edit code on a branch, commit it, and the pipeline builds and tests it. A passing change is merged, packaged into an image with a version tag, pushed to a registry and rolled out to the cluster.
Monitoring then confirms that users are better off, and if not, the rollout is undone.

The lab below is that flow in miniature. The sandbox understands git, ci, docker and kubectl. The checklist gives the destination, not the route: use what you have learned. If you get stuck, press Hint for the commands.

You now have the shape of modern delivery. The next steps are practice on real tools: set up a pipeline in a hosted service, deploy a container to a small cluster and watch its metrics. The ideas will carry over to every tool you meet.
